title: Single-exponential dependence on dimension for integer programming
formal: Do constants \(C,c>0\) and a deterministic algorithm exist that decide whether \(Ax\le b\) has an integer solution \(x\in \mathbb{Z} ^{n}\) in at most \(2^{Cn}(\mathrm{L}+1)^{c}\) bit operations, for every rational matrix A and vector b?
definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. A has m rows and n columns, both dimensions are part of the input, and the system need not be bounded. No limit on coefficient size, number of constraints or lattice width is promised. This target concerns feasibility.

context_blocks.text: Integer programming is polynomial-time solvable in every fixed dimension, but the dependence on dimension determines how far that tractability extends. The single-exponential target would make the geometric dimension cost comparable to exhaustive search over a constant-size choice per variable.

The 2025 survey records the Reis–Rothvoss bound \((\log  n)^{O(n)}\cdot \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L})\) and explicitly identifies \(2^{O(n)}\cdot \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L})\) as open. Here n is the number of integer variables, not the coefficient bit length. The question applies to unrestricted systems rather than one block-structured subclass.

why: Close the central dimension-dependence gap in a general-purpose optimization primitive used throughout parameterized algorithms.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
